Issued at 126 AM CDT Thu Sep 3 2026

Early this morning, there is warm frontal boundary sitting over 
portions of SD. The warm front, in addition to a bit of instability 
(RAP shows 1000-2000 J/kg along the boundary) are helping some 
isolated showers and storms to form and move over portions of 
central and northeastern SD. While a low level jet over north 
central is helping to provide some shear to sustain the storms for a 
bit, there is still a strong cap over the area that is helping to 
stop the storms from becoming to large and severe. The showers and 
storms should stay below severe criteria. However, with stronger 
DCAPE values (over 1000 J/kg) currently over central and 
northeastern SD, some stronger wind gusts could make it to the 
ground especially as the showers and storms are dissipating. These 
showers and storms should be gone by mid-morning. 

Southerly winds today will help to push warm, moist air into central 
and northeastern SD, with high temperatures in the mid 80s to low 
90s. This will help to create a nice environment for showers and 
storms to develop, with the models showing CAPE values of 1000-3000+ 
J/kg over northeastern SD this afternoon and evening. An upper-level 
shortwave moving over SD this afternoon will help to support a lee 
of the Rockies surface trough moving into central and northeastern 
SD, which could provide a source of lift. However, the warmer 
temperatures moving in aloft will help to create an inversion which 
will cap the environment to storm development. Models show the 
temperatures at 850 mph getting up between 20-26 degrees C over 
northeastern SD and west central MN, which will be hard to overcome. 
Due to this cap and the inversion, the models vary what could 
happen, lowering confidence in the storm chances late this afternoon 
into tonight. Some models have scattered showers and storms develop 
in ND, where there are some cooler temperatures aloft that the 
storms are able to overcome. These storms start more discreet as 
they move southeast into far northeastern SD and west central MN 
before moving east during the evening and becoming more of a line of 
storms. Other models have the warm front moving a bit slower, which 
could then cause storms to try and develop to the south and 
southeast of the forecasting area. These storms will then stay out 
of northeastern SD and west central MN. In either scenario, there 
will be mid-level lapse rates between 6-8 C/km and bulk shear values 
of 35-45 kts over northeastern SD and west central MN. If storms do 
develop or move into this environment, they will be capable of 
producing large hail and strong winds. Because of the cap that could 
prevent storms from developing, SPC has shifted the slight risk out 
of far northeastern SD and west central MN and moved the marginal 
risk to only cover those areas. The primary threats from the storms 
will still be hail up to 2 inches in diameter and wind gusts of 60-
70 mph if anything were to develop. The threat for storms should 
move out of the area during the late evening. 

Friday and into the weekend, an upper-level ridge is forecast to 
start developing to the south and over parts of SD. This will help 
to move some warmer temperatures into central and northeastern SD. 
Temperatures will be 10 to 20 degrees warmer than normal, with highs 
in the mid 80s to mid 90s. During Friday and through the weekend, 
upper-level shortwaves are forecast to move along the top of the 
ridge, which will be situated over central and northeastern SD, 
helping with shower and storm development. Some models forecast some 
drier air moving in Friday for the day, which could help to keep 
showers and storms from developing. However, other models have some 
moisture moving in Friday evening and overnight. In these models, as 
another frontal boundary tries to move through during that time, 
some scattered showers and storms then look to develop over central 
SD overnight into Saturday morning. The NAM forecasts there to be 
1000-2000 J/kg CAPE values over the area during Friday night which 
will help with storm development along the frontal boundary, but 
there does also look to be a bit of a cap from warmer temperatures 
aloft that will have to be overcome for things to develop. A low 
level jet looks to develop Friday night, which will help to support 
the longevity of the storms. Lapse rates of 6-7 C/km will help with 
some hail development in these storms, though most of them look to 
stay below the severe threshold.
